title: GPU runtime profiling: TensorRT-LLM vs vLLM, CUDA graphs
summary: Deep dive on GPU runtime profiling. Compared kernel selection behavior between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, looked at CUDA Graphs stability, KV cache handling, batching trade-offs, and on-prem/VPC deployment considerations. Agreed to run a 5h benchmark on Quantify's 8xA100 infra; Redwood to share profiling scripts and benchmark spreadsheet.
transcript:
Meeting header
Date: 2026-02-27
Time: 08:35 - 09:37 UTC
Duration: 62 minutes
Attendees: Elena Martinez (Redwood AE), Samir Patel (Redwood SE), Jules Nguyen (Redwood PM), Dr. Priya Kapoor (Quantify Labs), Marcus Lee (Quantify Labs SRE), Anton B. (Quantify Labs CTO)

Summary: quick technical deep dive to validate perf claims; focus on kernel selection differences between TensorRT-LLM and vLLM, how CUDA Graphs impacted latency tail, and KV cache/batching interplay. Action items at end.

[00:00:03] Elena (Redwood): Hey everyone, thanks for joining, quick roll call, and then Samir will dig into the profiler outputs we shared.
[00:00:12] Priya (Quantify): Hi, Priya here, Marcus and Anton are with me.
[00:00:18] Samir (Redwood): Great, so I put the slides and the profiling tarball in the shared folder — link in the chat — but i'll start with a high-level: we ran identical model checkpoints on TensorRT-LLM and vLLM with the same prompt distribution, on an 8xA100 setup, and instrumented kernel launches, cudaGraph captures, and KV hits.
[00:00:43] Marcus: quick question, are these FP16 runs or do you include quantized int8? that matters for TRT obviously.
[00:00:51] Samir: Mostly FP16 for parity; we also ran int8 via TRT INT8 quant for a subset, results later. The main difference we saw was kernel selection — TRT picks fused attention kernels aggressively, which reduces kernel launch overhead but is less flexible for variable sequence lengths.
[00:01:12] Priya: when you say fused kernels, do you mean the fused attention+softmax kernels? We saw some instability when sequence length jumps cause recompile.
[00:01:23] Samir: yeah, exactly. TRT's autotune path will choose a fused kernel if it matches the pair of seqlen and head dims; that gives 10-25% token throughput improvement in steady-state but triggers a fallback to generic kernels on mismatch which spikes latency.
[00:01:40] Elena: and that's where cudaGraph prewarming helps, right? to avoid per-request kernel launch jitter?
[00:01:46] Samir: partly. CUDA graphs capture the launch sequence, which helps reduce CPU overhead on the hot path; but graphs are brittle if the execution graph changes (different seqlen or kv cache state). We saw cases where cudaGraph had to be recreated, causing a small rollout hiccup.
[00:02:05] Priya: hmm, our workload is chatty with variable seqlen — context windows vary a lot — so recreating graphs might be non-trivial. Did you measure recreation cost?
[00:02:14] Samir: yes, we measured recreation time ~120-300ms depending on kernel compile path and whether TRT needs to re-autotune. vLLM path avoided runtime recompiles because it relies on many smaller kernels and just-in-time scheduling; it's more consistent but slightly lower peak throughput.
[00:02:32] Marcus: can you share the distribution of extreme p95/p99 latencies? that's our current SLO concern.
[00:02:38] Samir: sure, in the spreadsheet we posted: TRT FP16 steady-state p95 ~ 85ms, p99 ~ 230ms under bursty seqlen spikes where kernel fallback occurred. vLLM FP16 p95 ~ 110ms, p99 ~ 160ms. So TRT wins on p50 and steady throughput, vLLM is more stable on tail.
[00:02:59] Anton: interesting — so it's a tradeoff: max throughput vs tail stability. For on-prem, we care about both because we can't autoscale easily.
[00:03:08] Samir: Exactly. We also tested KV cache warm vs cold: TRT benefits more from large contiguous KV because fused kernels assume dense memory access; vLLM's cache sharding is more tolerant when KV is sparse.
[00:03:22] Priya: do you have recommendations for batching? our burstiness leads to lots of small batches with high latency.
[00:03:28] Samir: we suggested adaptive batching in the doc: small-batch fastpath for low-latency interactive, plus a background aggregator for throughput. On TRT, batching improves token throughput significantly, but you pay in tail latency if you wait to fill batches.
[00:03:43] Elena: we also recommend prefix caching for repeated system prompts to reduce per-request decode work.
[00:03:49] Priya: how does quantization affect kernel selection — does TRT select different kernels for int8?
[00:03:55] Samir: yes, TRT will select int8-specialized kernels and often has different autotune candidates. For some layers int8 gives big speedups; but accuracy/regression risk exists — we ran evals and saw small degradation on some tasks, so it's workload dependent.
[00:04:10] Marcus: what about memory pressure and multi-tenant isolation on a VPC/on-prem box?
[00:04:17] Samir: memory is the big one — TRT fused kernels can use more temp memory; we include a memory plan tool in the repo to model KV vs activation vs temp workspace. For multi-tenant we recommend strict cgroup/GPU partitioning and preallocating KV cache pools.
[00:04:33] Priya: the repo — is it public or do we get a copy?
[00:04:37] Elena: we'll share the profiling scripts and the sample infra-as-code we used. Link: https://redwood-internal.s3/benchmarks/qlabs-2026-02-27
[00:04:46] Priya: perfect.
[00:04:52] [05:00] Samir: jumping into a profiler screenshot — you'll see a long flat green block where TRT runs fused attention, very high GPU occupancy, then small yellow spikes when kernels fallback. here's the rough timeline: graph capture -> steady decode -> fallback event -> re-autotune.
[00:05:18] Priya: can you correlate fallback events to specific requests? we'd like to route those to a lower-priority queue.
[00:05:25] Samir: yes, we log kernel selection events with request ids in the trace; we can add a rule to route requests that would trigger fallback to vLLM or a safer model variant.
[00:05:39] Marcus: what's the effort to set up the routing logic? does the Redwood runtime support policy-based routing today?
[00:05:45] Elena: yes, smart routing exists in the platform: you can define policy by latency, cost, region; we'll add a rule type for kernel-fallback signals as discussed.
[00:05:56] Priya: nice. On the CUDA Graphs note — if graph capture fails due to variable seqlen, any recommended heuristics?
[00:06:03] Samir: a few: 1) bucket requests by seqlen and create a small number of graphs, 2) capture graphs for the common hot paths and fallback to non-graph execution for odd requests, 3) prewarm graphs during low-traffic windows.
[00:06:18] Anton: curious about reproducibility — TRT autotune can be non-deterministic across runs — did you encounter that?
[00:06:24] Samir: we did see some variance, especially with mixed workload, so we recommend freezing kernel selection in production after a controlled calibration run and store the selected kernels to avoid re-autotune in-situ.
[00:06:36] Priya: how does model sharding behave across nodes for KV cache? our chat history is large and we want to avoid cross-node KV fetches.
[00:06:44] Samir: we recommend client-level affinity: pin users to a pod with their KV shard, and use local disk-based caching for long histories. For cross-node fetches, latency kills you; so locality is key.
[00:06:58] Marcus: do you support disk-backed KV cache with eviction policies in Redwood Private?
[00:07:03] Elena: yes, Redwood Private supports pluggable KV backends; you can use local SSD + LRU eviction, or external vectorstore with strong affinity guarantees.
[00:07:13] Priya: what's the best way to stress test our on-prem infra to mimic production chat load?
[00:07:18] Samir: use the benchmark harness included; run mixed prompt distributions, instrument kernel selection logs, and replay real user traces. We can help run an initial 5-hour benchmark on your 8xA100 as a POC.
[00:07:30] Anton: what's the expected time to run that POC and what do you need from our side?
[00:07:35] Elena: we need SSH access to a bastion (read-only), a small service account for monitoring, and a baseline dataset of prompts. We'll run the benchmark, collect traces, and produce a report.
[00:07:46] Priya: ok, security wise we need SOC2 artifacts — can you share your SOC2 report and network diagram?
[00:07:52] Elena: yes, we'll attach SOC2 and the network architecture doc to the follow-up email.
[00:07:58] [25:00] Samir: quick note on quantization: for int8 we saw memory drop ~30% and token throughput up to 1.8x in TRT on some models; but on vLLM quantized kernels gains were smaller due to less specialized int8 paths.
[00:08:15] Priya: And model fidelity after quant? did you run evals?
[00:08:19] Samir: yes, small eval suite — most tasks within 1-2% of baseline, a few classification/regression tasks dropped more; we flagged those in the spreadsheet.
[00:08:27] Marcus: any special config for A100s to get stable performance? PCIe/NVLink config, MIG? we use 4 x A100S with NVLink.
[00:08:35] Samir: NVLink helps KV transfer; avoid MIG for big-model serving (MIG slices can starve memory). Preallocate memory pools and pin CUDA contexts per-serving process.
[00:08:48] Priya: what about observability — can we get per-request kernel-level traces in Redwood Console?
[00:08:54] Elena: yes, we can surface kernel selection events, cudaGraph re-creates, and per-token latencies; we'll enable a custom dashboard for your account during the POC.
[00:09:06] [40:00] Samir: last technical callouts: 1) bucket seqlens, 2) prewarm graphs, 3) freeze kernels after calibration, 4) have fallback policy to vLLM for tail stability, 5) consider int8 for throughput if your evals pass.
[00:09:28] Priya: that's great; can you also add guidance for rolling kernel updates? we don't want to hit regressions on deploy.
[00:09:35] Samir: absolutely—canary kernel rollout, A/B traffic split, and automated quality regressions tied to eval sets.
[00:09:45] Elena: ok let's recap next steps.
[00:09:49] Priya: go ahead.
[00:09:52] Elena: next steps: Redwood to share profiling scripts and benchmark harness, schedule the 5-hour POC on Quantify's infra, provide SOC2 and network docs, and we'll add a routing rule prototype for kernel-fallback. Marcus — you'll share access details and the prompt dataset.
[00:10:10] Marcus: will do, aiming to get access by next Monday.
[00:10:14] Anton: timeline looks good.
[00:10:17] Elena: thanks everyone, we'll follow up with a calendar invite and the artifacts.

End transcript (notes: transcription contains minor errors and occasional speaker mis-attribution).
